newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Once-feared Khmer Rouge cornered in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Once-feared Khmer Rouge cornered in Cambodia.

text.p: The despised Pol Pot and his communist Khmer Rouge guerrillas, who have terrorised Cambodia for more than 20 years, have met a humbling end in the jungles where they once lurked.

Co-premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen announced on Saturday that notorious rebel strongman Pol Pot had been arrested by renegades from his own splintered army and would eventually face trial to answer for the crimes of his 1975-79 "killing fields" regime.
"We won't have any problems with the Khmer Rouge any more," said member of parlaiment Ahmad Yahya.
"This is the end of war in Cambodia... It is a happy ending," another member of parliament, Om Radsady, told Reuters.

In a rare moment of agreement, Cambodia's feuding premiers confirmed Pol Pot's capture as they stood elbow to elbow outside a government hall where they had just welcomed visiting Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh.
"If they declared this side-by-side, it means they definitely have Pol Pot," Om Radsady said.

The two premiers, embroiled in a bitter power struggle for months, were sharply divided over policy toward the rebels with both men trying to gain political advantage as the rebel force self-destructed.
Saturday's joint announcement led even the most sceptical analysts to finally believe that Pol Pot was finished.
"Having both prime ministers say this lends substance," said a military analyst. "I'm 90 percent (sure)... If we don't get him alive, we'll be getting him some way or another."

Pol Pot, whose ultra-leftist regime left more than one million Cambodians dead, fled his northern stronghold of Anlong Veng earlier this month after executing his defence chief and 11 of his family members.
His Khmer Rouge army has been decimated by government attacks and thousands of defections since they boycotted a U.N.-supervised election in 1993.

Last August, the Khmer Rouge was riven by its most serious split ever when commanders in its western zone, who had grown rich on the spoils of black market trade, rejected Pol Pot's communism and defected to the government.

Pol Pot and his hard-core followers continued their low-intensity war against the coalition government from Cambodia's dense northern jungles until earlier this month when the remnants of the group was hit by a bloody split.
In the end, Pol Pot was left with only a handful of fighters at his side, holed up in a jungle camp ringed with landmines, as his former comrades closed in to capture him.
The two premiers said the breakaway group would be incorporated into government forces.
"This is the end of the Khmer Rouge," Hun Sen told reporters.
Some analysts thought it significant that the news of Pol Pot's capture came during the Thai premier's visit.

Thailand was a key suporter of the Khmer Rouge in the 1980s when it and two allied, non-communist guerrilla groups battled a Vietnamese army of occupation and the Hanoi-backed government in Phnom Penh.

"The Thais have been actively involved since the beginning. It's not by chance that Chavalit is here or that the co-premiers made the statement expressing a common view after their meeting," said a scholar of the Khmer Rouge.

Ranariddh and Hun Sen had exchanged bitter words over whether to make peace with the hard-liners. Ranariddh favoured talks, but Hun Sen, apparently fearing an imminent political alliance between the prince and the rebels, called all negotiations illegal.
"They needed to convey this message, that they were working together. It's a positive development," a diplomat from the region told Reuters.
But few believe the truce between the two leaders will last too long.
"They could be at each other's throats as soon as Chavalit leaves," said a foreign political analyst.
